clue.text: "It has no kind of fault or flaw / And, my Lords, — the Law" (W. S. Gilbert)

definitions.text: "It has no kind of fault or flaw / And, my Lords, — the Law" (W. S. Gilbert)

parts.words: "It has no kind of fault or flaw / And, my Lords, — the Law" (W. S. Gilbert)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the Lord Chancellor's song in Gilbert's Iolanthe, where he claims to personify the law itself

explanation.surface: A line of Gilbert and Sullivan with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The song in Iolanthe runs 'The Law is the true embodiment of everything that's excellent… And I, my Lords, — the Law'; the missing verb echoes that earlier noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To personify or give physical form to something is the verb the Lord Chancellor uses for himself and the legal system.

clue.text: And more Latin from Birrell

explanation.surface: Further Latin borrowed from an essayist.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'and the rest'; it is also the title of a 1930 collection of essays by Augustine Birrell.

clue.text: Support for writers, in conclusion

explanation.surface: Help for authors, to finish off.
explanation.definitionFit: A prop that holds a row of volumes upright supports writers' works; read literally, the close of a volume is where it concludes.

clue.text: Tragically betrayed wife shows spirit in new edition of Sade

indicators.note: the spirit sits inside the rearranged letters
a new edition reworks the text, so the letters of the name Sade are rearranged

parts.note: a demon is an evil spirit

explanation.surface: A tragic wife appears as a ghost in a reissue of the Marquis de Sade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new edition of' looks like publishing talk but signals rearrangement; Sade is the Marquis de Sade, not a word to take literally. The wife is Othello's.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's wife is falsely accused through Iago's scheming and murdered by her husband in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: First man on barrage as Stevenson protagonist

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece placed on another follows it

parts.note: Adam is the first man in Genesis
a barrage is a dam or weir across a river

explanation.surface: Biblical Adam standing on a dam, recast as a Stevenson hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Archie's father, Lord Hermiston, is the title figure of Weir of Hermiston, Stevenson's unfinished last novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The hanging judge Lord Hermiston is the central figure of Robert Louis Stevenson's unfinished novel Weir of Hermiston.

clue.text: 9's chiaroscuro?

parts.note: the painter's term for contrast of light and shade, applied to a novel title by the author at 9-down

explanation.surface: An art term for light and dark, attached to another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivy Compton-Burnett (9-down) published a novel in 1951 whose title pairs night and its opposite, the contrast chiaroscuro describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Chiaroscuro is the play of light against shadow, which this Compton-Burnett title spells out in words.

clue.text: One very close in fielding?

parts.note: reads like a cricket fielder stationed near the batsman; really someone 'close' with money, i.e. stingy

explanation.surface: A cricket fielder posted right next to the bat.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, 'close' fielders stand near the batsman; here 'close' means tight-fisted.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder who refuses to spend is called close-fisted, so very close in the money sense.

clue.text: "The public — —/ Hath offered that these Lays other efforts 7 surpass" (William Henry Ireland)

definitions.text: "The public — —/ Hath offered that these Lays other efforts 7 surpass" (William Henry Ireland)

parts.words: "The public — —/ Hath offered that these Lays other efforts 7 surpass" (William Henry Ireland)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the Shakespeare forger Ireland, the blanks being a French phrase meaning all together

explanation.surface: A couplet by a notorious forger with a phrase missing, used twice.
explanation.walkthrough: The '7' inside the quotation refers back to this entry, so the same phrase fills both gaps.
explanation.definitionFit: The borrowed French phrase means all at once, as a whole body of people.

clue.text: Hopkins personality, called happy (in fine fettle?), now deceased

definitions.text: Hopkins personality, called happy (in fine fettle?), now deceased

parts.words: Hopkins personality, called happy (in fine fettle?), now deceased
parts.note: the farrier of a Gerard Manley Hopkins poem, whose first name is Latin for happy, who 'fettled' horseshoes and has died when the poem opens

explanation.surface: A character from Hopkins, cheerful and healthy, but now dead.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem opens 'Felix Randal the farrier, O is he dead then?'; Felix is Latin for happy, and he fettled 'the bright and battering sandal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Felix is the farrier's forename, so the surname is what remains of the poem's title character.

clue.text: "Ivy never sere", no doubt, to devotees

definitions.text: "Ivy never sere", no doubt, to devotees

parts.words: "Ivy never sere", no doubt, to devotees
parts.note: ivy is evergreen and never withers; admirers would say the same of the novelist Ivy whose reputation endures

explanation.surface: Fans declaring that a plant never withers.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivy Compton-Burnett was an English novelist; 'sere' means dried up and withered.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist's first name is the evergreen climber, so her fans call her undying.

clue.text: That of Hawaii proved fatal to the navigator

definitions.text: That of Hawaii proved fatal to the navigator

parts.words: That of Hawaii proved fatal to the navigator
parts.note: Captain James Cook was killed in Hawaii in 1779 during his third voyage

explanation.surface: A trip to Hawaii that killed a famous explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means a quick sightseeing trip, after Thomas Cook's travel firm; here it is Captain Cook's actual voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Cook's last expedition ended with his death at Kealakekua Bay, so his visit to the islands was fatal.

clue.text: Rosemary Sutcliffe's apostle?

explanation.surface: Asking which disciple a children's novelist wrote about.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary Sutcliff wrote a 1953 novel of that name, and Simon Peter and Simon the Zealot were two of the twelve disciples.

clue.text: Main subject of Benchley

explanation.surface: The principal topic of a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea, and Peter Benchley wrote a novel about the ocean titled so.

clue.text: Venetian barrister's clerk as siren, quite wild

indicators.note: the letters of the two words run wild into a new order

explanation.surface: A Venetian legal clerk behaving like a wild temptress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite wild' shuffles AS and SIREN. In The Merchant of Venice Portia's maid disguises herself as clerk to Portia's sham lawyer.
explanation.definitionFit: Portia's waiting-woman poses as the clerk of the young doctor of law in Shakespeare's Venice play.

clue.text: Like Keillor's affair

parts.note: Garrison Keillor's novel WLT: A ___ Romance is about a broadcasting station, and also describes his long career on air

explanation.surface: Comparing something to a writer's love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: Keillor, the American humorist of A Prairie Home Companion, wrote the novel 'WLT: A Radio Romance' (1991).
explanation.definitionFit: Keillor's romance in the novel title is a broadcasting one, so the blank word describes that sort of affair.

clue.text: One watching former pupil and member of waiting staff

parts.note: OB, old boy, is a former pupil of a school
a server is a waiter at table

explanation.surface: An old schoolboy who now works as a waiter keeps an eye on things.
explanation.walkthrough: OB (old boy) is the British term for a former pupil of a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who watches is an onlooker or spectator.

clue.text: Seen accompanying friends in Bowen book

definitions.text: Seen accompanying friends in Bowen book

parts.words: Seen accompanying friends in Bowen book
parts.note: Elizabeth Bowen's 1931 novel title is Friends and ___, so the word comes after friends

explanation.surface: Something spotted alongside friends in a novel by Elizabeth Bowen.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Bowen was an Anglo-Irish novelist; her 1931 novel is 'Friends and Relations'.
explanation.definitionFit: Family members complete the title alongside friends, as in the stock phrase for one's whole circle.

clue.text: "On a winter's afternoon, in a — chapel / History is now and England" (T. S. Eliot)

definitions.text: "On a winter's afternoon, in a — chapel / History is now and England" (T. S. Eliot)

parts.words: "On a winter's afternoon, in a — chapel / History is now and England" (T. S. Eliot)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Little Gidding, the last of Eliot's Four Quartets, about the remote chapel there

explanation.surface: A line of Eliot about a winter chapel with one word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The chapel at Little Gidding is remote and hidden away, the adjective Eliot uses for it.

clue.text: Palatial interior of Balham brassiere shop

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of two words

explanation.surface: A grand lingerie shop in Balham, south London.
explanation.walkthrough: Balham is a district of south London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Moorish palace-fortress in Granada is the definition's suggestion of something palace-like.

clue.text: Disturbed at sleep in French novel

indicators.note: disturbed sleep is broken up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A French novel read when sleep will not come.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed' shuffles AT SLEEP into Camus's novel of an epidemic in Oran.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Camus's 1947 book about plague in Algeria is a novel written in French.

clue.text: Oriel opens out on to French flower

indicators.note: the window's letters unfold into a new order

explanation.surface: A bay window opening onto a French bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opens out' rearranges ORIEL. A 'flower' in crosswords is often something that flows: a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The longest river in France flows to the Atlantic, so it is a 'flow-er'.

clue.text: Deduce no Dantean vision

parts.note: to deduce is to infer

explanation.surface: Concluding that something is not Dante's vision.
explanation.definitionFit: The first part of the Divine Comedy is Dante's imagined journey through Hell.

clue.text: Heads were broken in Athenian street violence

definitions.text: Heads were broken in Athenian street violence

parts.words: Heads were broken in Athenian street violence
parts.note: in 415 BC the stone pillars topped with heads of the god Hermes that stood in Athens streets were mutilated overnight

explanation.surface: A report of skulls cracked in a riot in ancient Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'heads' are not people's but the carved heads on the Herms, the boundary pillars whose mutilation caused a scandal before the Sicilian expedition.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of a Greek pillar topped with a bust of Hermes, the street markers that were defaced.

clue.text: Colin Thubron's novel concerto

explanation.surface: A novel by a travel writer, and a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: Thubron's 1978 novel bears this title, as does Beethoven's fifth piano concerto, so named for its grandeur.

clue.text: Pole with fashionable following becomes French artist

indicators.note: the second piece comes after the first

parts.note: a rod is a pole
in means fashionable

explanation.surface: A Pole who becomes a trendy French artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' with a capital looks like a nationality; it is a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Rodin was the French sculptor of The Thinker.

clue.text: Obedient as Keneally's child

explanation.surface: A well-behaved youngster from an Australian novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Obedient means compliant and dutiful; Thomas Keneally's 1971 novel is A Dutiful Daughter, so his child is so described.

clue.text: Pondered note on goddess

indicators.note: the note is placed after the goddess

parts.note: a Muse is one of nine goddesses of the arts
D is a musical note

explanation.surface: Thinking about a musical note dedicated to a goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder is to reflect or think deeply.

clue.text: Titania thought she was of an ass

definitions.text: Titania thought she was of an ass

parts.words: Titania thought she was of an ass
parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the fairy queen, under a love potion, dotes on Bottom wearing an ass's head

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's fairy queen judging herself foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thought she was … of an ass' suggests she thought herself an ass; really she was in love with one.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in love with someone, the state the potion causes in the fairy queen.

clue.text: Vaughan spotted it the other night

definitions.text: Vaughan spotted it the other night

parts.words: Vaughan spotted it the other night
parts.note: Henry Vaughan's poem The World opens 'I saw ___ the other night, / Like a great ring of pure and endless light'

explanation.surface: A poet claiming to have glimpsed something recently.
explanation.definitionFit: The metaphysical poet saw endless time as a great ring of pure light.

clue.text: Demons exorcized by Thackeray

indicators.note: the demons are driven out of their shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Thackeray drives out evil spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exorcized' rearranges DEMONS into Thackeray's historical novel The History of Henry ___.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's 1852 historical novel is named after its hero Henry, so the title is a work written by him.
